records.place: Magill, Adelaide; Grange is drawn from across South Australia

wine.name: Grange
wine.grapes: Shiraz, the great majority, often with a small share of Cabernet Sauvignon.
wine.sites: No single site: Shiraz from several South Australian regions, the Barossa Valley above all, with McLaren Vale, the Clare Valley and, in some years, the Magill Estate vineyard in Adelaide.
wine.making: Fermented on its skins in tanks with header boards, wooden boards that keep the cap under the juice, the wine is racked into new American oak hogsheads to finish its fermentation and then matures in them for sixteen to twenty one months, by vintage, before bottling.
wine.glass: Mocha and vanilla from new American oak over blackberry, black plum and mulberry, with liquorice and dark chocolate; full in body and dense, with ripe, firm tannin, fresh acidity and a lasting finish with a graphite edge.
wine.ageing: Tight and oaky for its first ten years or so, it opens slowly; the house gives a strong vintage a drinking window that runs forty years and more.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for two hours or more, an old one gently off its sediment; a large Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The bin number Grange carries, a house code from the cellar rather than a legal classification.
The state appellation, wide enough to cover a blend from several of its regions.
The grape the label names; up to the 1989 vintage the wine was sold as Grange Hermitage.

records.table: Penfolds blends Grange from Shiraz grown across South Australia rather than on one site, finishes it in barrel and ages it in new American oak. Dense, with blackberry, mocha and liquorice, it needs many years; decant it and pour it into a large glass.
records.story: The flagship takes its name from The Grange, the stone cottage at Magill, east of Adelaide, where Dr Christopher Rawson Penfold (1811 to 1870), an English physician, settled with his wife in 1844. After his death in 1870 his wife ran the winery, and the house grew on fortified wine. In 1948 Max Schubert (1915 to 1994) became its first chief winemaker, and a visit to Bordeaux in 1950 set him on a red that could live for twenty years and more. He made the first Grange, experimentally, in 1951 from Shiraz grown at Magill and Morphett Vale; it was never sold commercially, and the 1952 was the first vintage released. When senior management tasted the early vintages in 1957 they ordered him to stop, and he made the 1957, 1958 and 1959 in secret in the Magill cellars. Retasted with some age, the early wines changed the board's mind, and production resumed openly with the 1960 vintage. The wine carried the name Grange Hermitage, Hermitage being an old Australian name for Shiraz, up to the 1989 vintage, and it has been made in every vintage since 1951. In 2001, fifty years on, the National Trust of South Australia listed it as a heritage icon. Its counterpart is Henschke's Hill of Grace: one Shiraz blended across regions, the other grown on one hill.

others.name: Bin 389 Cabernet Shiraz
others.note: Matured in barrels that held the previous vintage of Grange, hence its nickname, Baby Grange.

Grange Hermitage and Grange are one wine: Hermitage, an old Australian name for Shiraz, left the label with the 1990 vintage.

records.place: Keyneton, Eden Valley, Barossa, South Australia

wine.name: Hill of Grace
wine.grapes: Shiraz alone, from vines on their own roots.
wine.sites: The Hill of Grace vineyard near Keyneton, facing the Gnadenberg Lutheran church at about 400 metres; its oldest Shiraz, the Grandfathers, dates from about 1860, dry grown and ungrafted on red-brown earth that grades into deep silty loam.
wine.making: Fermented in open fermenters, as the hand picked first vintage of 1958 was, the wine matures for eighteen to twenty months in oak hogsheads before blending and bottling; the barrels are French above all, with a little American oak in some years, and the share of new wood changes widely by vintage.
wine.glass: Five spice, star anise, sage and black pepper over blackberry, black plum and blueberry, with cedar from the barrel; perfumed rather than heavy, with velvety, fine-grained tannin, lively acidity and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Worth leaving for several years after release, it grows more savoury for decades; by the house's reckoning a well cellared bottle of a strong year lasts thirty years and more.
wine.serve: In a large red wine glass, at 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or so, and an old one gently off its sediment.

label.means: The English for Gnadenberg, the name of the Lutheran church facing the vineyard, taken from a region of Silesia.
The higher, cooler region of the Barossa zone, an appellation of its own, separate from the Barossa Valley.

records.table: Facing the Gnadenberg church at Keyneton, in Eden Valley, Henschke's Hill of Grace is Shiraz whose oldest vines date from about 1860. Plum, five spice and sage over fine tannin give it perfume more than weight: the single vineyard answer to Grange.
records.story: Keyneton, in the hills east of the Barossa Valley, was called North Rhine when the family's founder, a stonemason and wheelwright from Silesia, settled there; he had reached South Australia in 1841 and farmed first in the Adelaide Hills and at Krondorf. He planted a small vineyard and made his first wine there in 1868. Close by, around 1860, a settler had planted Shiraz on land beside the Lutheran church of Gnadenberg, the Hill of Grace, and in 1891 the founder's son bought the land with its vines; he was the church's organist for many years. For decades the family made mostly fortified wine for sale in bulk. Cyril Henschke (1924 to 1979), of the fourth generation, turned the house towards dry table wine and towards wine of one vineyard: Mount Edelstone came first, and Hill of Grace followed with the 1958 vintage, hand picked and fermented in open vats. South Australia never had phylloxera, so the oldest block, the Grandfathers, grows on its own roots, and the vineyard came through the state's vine pull scheme of the 1980s, which uprooted a great deal of old Barossa Shiraz. After Cyril's death in 1979 the fifth generation took the house on. Hill of Grace and Grange are the pair a sommelier learns together, one vineyard set against a blend of many.

The vineyard lies too high for any vine pest

records.place: Krondorf Road, Tanunda, Barossa Valley, South Australia

wine.name: Basket Press Shiraz
wine.sites: Small parcels of old, dry grown Shiraz, most of them bought from grower families across the Barossa Valley, some of the vines more than a century old.
wine.making: Made on restored old equipment, much of it from the nineteenth century and salvaged as other cellars modernised: the fruit is fermented in open fermenters and pressed slowly and gently in a basket press about a century old, then matured in seasoned French and American oak, hogsheads above all with some larger vats, before bottling.
wine.glass: Blackberry, black plum and mulberry with dark chocolate, black pepper and a tarry, earthy note of forest floor; full in body, with velvety tannin from the gentle press and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Its first years are tight and tannic; it then softens and gains depth over a decade or more in the cellar.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius, in a large red wine glass; a young bottle wants an hour in a decanter, an older one careful decanting off its sediment.

label.means: Pressed in an old basket press, the method the wine is named for, not a vineyard.
The appellation of the warm valley floor, as distinct from the higher Eden Valley.

records.table: Old vine Shiraz bought from Barossa Valley grower families goes into Rockford's Basket Press Shiraz, fermented in open vats and pressed in a century old basket press. With blackberry, chocolate and black pepper on a full, velvety body, it shows the Barossa as it was made before modern machinery.
records.story: Rockford grew from a property on Krondorf Road near Tanunda, bought by its founder in 1971, with a stone cottage and outbuildings of the 1850s from the early settlement of Krondorf. The winery was put together from restored old equipment, open fermenters and basket presses among it, much of it of the nineteenth century and salvaged as other cellars modernised, and in 1984 the founder made the first Basket Press Shiraz, Rockford's first vintage. The timing went against the market. In the mid 1980s, in a glut of grapes, the South Australian government paid growers to pull out their vines, and the Barossa lost much of its old Shiraz and Grenache. Rockford bought instead from the growers who had kept their old, dry grown vines, and built the house on its ties with those families more than on vines of its own. The wine became the traditionalist's Barossa Shiraz: slow basket pressing, open vats and a wine of texture rather than force. Its sparkling red, Black Shiraz, made by the traditional method, gave the house a second following. When a guest asks what Barossa Shiraz tasted like before new oak and heavy extraction became its fashion, Basket Press is the bottle to open.

others.note: A sparkling red Shiraz made by the traditional method, dry to off dry, the house's other famous bottle.

wine.name: 100 Year Old Para Vintage Tawny
wine.grapes: Shiraz and Grenache, alone or together by vintage, from the estate's own Barossa vineyards, as the house describes its recent releases.
wine.sites: Barossa fruit; the wine is defined less by a vineyard than by the Centennial Cellar at Seppeltsfield, finished in 1878, where its cask rests for a century.
wine.making: Fermented and fortified with grape spirit while still sweet, as all the Para Tawnies are; a cask of each vintage is then laid down in the Centennial Cellar and left in wood for a hundred years, slowly concentrating, before it is bottled for release.
wine.glass: Treacle, walnut and burnt toffee with preserved fruit, exotic spice and the nutty tang of rancio; thick and intensely sweet, the sweetness held in check by concentration and a sharp volatile lift.
wine.ageing: Released ready to drink at a hundred years old; it needs no further cellaring.
wine.serve: 12 to 14 degrees Celsius, cool, as for an old tawny; no need to decant; a small white wine glass and a small measure, after dinner.

label.means: The wine spent a century in its cask in the Centennial Cellar before release.
All of it comes from the one harvest named on the label, never a blend of years.
A sweet fortified wine aged in wood; Australian wine no longer carries the name Port.

records.table: One Barossa harvest and a hundred years in cask: Seppeltsfield's 100 Year Old Para Vintage Tawny is a fortified wine released only when its century in the Centennial Cellar is done. Treacle, walnut and toffee, thick and sweet, it is poured in small measures after dinner.
records.story: Born in Lower Silesia, Joseph Ernst Seppelt (1813 to 1868) sailed for South Australia with his family in 1849, and in 1851, by the house's account, he founded the estate in the Barossa Valley that took his name. He died in 1868, and his eldest son, in his early twenties, took the business on and grew it. In 1878 the son completed the Centennial Cellar. That year he chose a puncheon, a large cask, of the estate's fortified wine and gave orders that it was not to be bottled for a hundred years. A cask from every vintage since has been laid down beside it, an unbroken line from 1878 to the present harvest. In 1978 the 1878 was released, a century old, and each year since the next vintage in the line has followed at a hundred years of age. When Australia agreed with the European Union to stop using the name Port, the house's Para wines went on as Tawny. It is history in a small glass: a wine laid down a century before it is poured, from a cellar where every year since 1878 waits its turn.

The 1878, released in 1978, began the series; the Centennial Cellar holds a cask of every vintage since.

wine.name: The Signature Cabernet Sauvignon Shiraz
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon and Shiraz, the share of each changing with the vintage.
wine.sites: Barossa vineyards, with Shiraz from vines planted as early as 1945; the first vintage, 1962, joined Eden Valley Shiraz to Cabernet Sauvignon from the house's Oxford Landing vineyard, by its own record.
wine.making: Matured for eighteen to twenty two months, by vintage, in hogsheads and barriques of French and Hungarian oak, with American oak in some earlier vintages and a fifth or so of the barrels new in recent ones; the first vintage, by the house's record, was raised in French puncheons. The house runs its own cooperage.
wine.glass: Smoke and a savoury note of grilled meat over blackcurrant, blackberry and plum; the Cabernet gives a frame of firm, fine tannin and the Shiraz flesh in the middle, and the finish is long and dry.
wine.ageing: Made to cellar, it stays closed and firm for its first years and opens slowly over a decade and more in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: A Bordeaux glass at 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; give a young bottle an hour in a decanter, and decant an old one gently off its sediment.

records.table: Each vintage of Yalumba's The Signature is dedicated to one person who has served the house, and the wine, made since 1962, is a Barossa blend of Cabernet Sauvignon and Shiraz. Firm Cabernet tannin frames its blackcurrant and plum, a red to lay down.
records.story: Two years after bringing his family to South Australia in 1847, Samuel Smith (1812 to 1889), a brewer from Wareham in Dorset, was working as a gardener at Angaston. That year he bought land of his own and named it Yalumba, by most accounts an Aboriginal word for all the land around; the story goes that he planted his first vines by moonlight, after his day's work on his employer's estate. The house traces itself to that planting and has stayed with his descendants, which makes it, by its own account, Australia's oldest family owned winery, and it keeps its own cooperage. The Signature began with the 1962 vintage, by the house's record a blend of Eden Valley Shiraz and Cabernet Sauvignon matured in French puncheons, and was first released in 1966. Each vintage is dedicated to one person who has given much to Yalumba, members of its staff among them, and more than fifty have been honoured so far. The blend has moved with the vineyards: the modern wine is drawn from the Barossa and raised in French and Hungarian oak. On a list it stands for the Cabernet Shiraz blend, a pairing Australia made its own, told through one family house and the people who served it.

traps: The Signature blends Cabernet Sauvignon and Shiraz; it is not a single varietal Shiraz like The Octavius.
The Signature's first vintage was 1962, but that wine was not released until 1966.
An octave is a small cask, not a vineyard or a blend term.

questions.exp: The Signature is a blend of Cabernet Sauvignon and Shiraz, the share of each changing with the vintage; it is raised in hogsheads and barriques, not old vats, and is a dry table wine.

report: One retailer's page says The Signature grew out of a Special Reserve Galway Claret of 1942, rebadged in 1962; the house's own pages make 1962 the first vintage and 1966 the first release, and the record follows the house.
The oak changes by vintage (2005: 22 months, French, American and Hungarian, 31 per cent new; 2022: 18 months; 2023: 19 months, 22 per cent new, French and Hungarian), so making gives the range.

Smith's arrival is August 1847 in Wikipedia and December 1847 in SA Memory, and the ADB's life summary gives Morden for his birthplace where its biography says Wareham; the record keeps the year and Wareham, which the biography and Wikipedia share.
The house counted more than 57 Signatories on its 2023 page, so more than fifty is a floor that stays true.
The make up of the 1962, Eden Valley Shiraz with Oxford Landing Cabernet in French puncheons, rests on the house's back vintage page alone and is told as its record.
The house's newer red, The Caley, could be argued as its flagship today; The Signature is kept for its sixty years of history, and no swap is proposed.

changed: story: his wife and five children becomes his family; the ADB gives five children, a brochure of the house's agent and a merchant four, and the state's pioneer vigneron profile has his first wife Mary and a second marriage in 1875, so the count is not kept.

story, wine.sites and wine.making: the make up and the oak of the 1962 are told as the house's record; no source outside the house's back vintage page names Eden Valley Shiraz, Oxford Landing or the French puncheons.
open: One merchant's account has the first Signature of 1962 labelled Galway Vintage Claret, with Samuel Smith as its signatory, and another has a Special Reserve Galway Claret of 1942 rebadged in 1962; the record follows the house's 1962 and 1966.
